prompt: `Loan`'s constructor printed `title=null` on its first line. Why `null`?
hint: What did the JVM do to the memory before anything else?

choices.text: Because `title` has no initialiser, the compiler inserts `title = null` at the end of the constructor
choices.why: Nothing is inserted at the end; the field was null before the constructor started.

choices.text: The object's memory starts zeroed
choices.why: Right: a reference field starts as `null`, a number as 0, a boolean as false.

choices.text: Because the argument had not been passed yet
choices.why: The argument was there; the constructor simply had not assigned it to the field yet.

prompt: Put the steps of `new Loan("Effective Java")` in the order they happen.
items: Memory for the object is reserved and zeroed
The reference is stored in the variable `loan`

prompt: In the bytecode of `main`, what is `<init>`?

choices.text: The instruction that allocates the object
choices.why: Allocation is the `new` instruction, which comes first.

choices.text: A hidden method that zeroes the fields
choices.why: Zeroing is part of `new`; `<init>` runs the code the class wrote.

choices.text: The constructor, compiled as a method
choices.why: Right: `invokespecial` runs it on the object `new` produced.

choices.text: The class's static initialiser
choices.why: That one is called `<clinit>` and runs once per class; lesson 27 shows it.

prompt: Why can a constructor rely on nobody else using the object while it runs?
hint: Where is the reference between `new` and `<init>`?

choices.text: Because the JVM locks every object until its constructor returns
choices.why: There is no such lock; nobody else simply has the reference yet.

choices.text: Until it returns, the only reference is the one being initialised; the caller stores it after
choices.why: Right: `astore_1` comes after `invokespecial`, so `loan` is set only once the constructor is done.

choices.text: Because fields cannot be read before the constructor's last line
choices.why: The constructor read three fields on its first line.

prompt: When does the garbage collector consider an object garbage?

choices.text: When the program has not used it for a while
choices.why: Use is not tracked; an unused object that is still reachable is kept.

choices.text: When the method that created it returns
choices.why: An object outlives its creating method whenever something reachable still points at it.

choices.text: When no chain of references reaches it from a root
choices.why: Right: that is the whole rule.

choices.text: When nothing at all points at it
choices.why: Two unreachable objects pointing at each other are still garbage.

prompt: Which of these are roots? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A local variable of a method that is still running
choices.why: Yes: `pages` in `main` kept every array of `Hoard` alive.

choices.text: A static field
choices.why: Yes: `latest` in `Churn` kept the newest array.

choices.text: A field of an object nothing reaches
choices.why: An unreachable object's fields lead nowhere the collector looks.

choices.text: A local variable of a method that has returned
choices.why: Once the method returns its frame is gone, and so is the variable.

prompt: `Churn` allocated how many megabytes, in a heap capped at 32 MB?
A `-Xlog:gc` line reads `Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 18M->1M(32M) 0.784ms`. What does `18M->1M(32M)` say?
hint: Before, after, and the size of the heap.

choices.text: 18 MB in use before, 1 MB after, in a 32 MB heap
choices.why: Right: almost everything was garbage.

choices.text: 18 objects collected, 1 kept, out of 32
choices.why: The numbers are megabytes, as the `M` says, not object counts.

choices.text: The heap grew from 18 MB to 32 MB and 1 MB was freed
choices.why: The heap stayed at 32 MB; the use fell from 18 to 1.

choices.text: The pause lasted 18 ms, and 1 ms of that was spent on the 32 MB heap
choices.why: The duration is the last field, 0.784 ms.

prompt: `Churn` allocated almost 2 GB in a 32 MB heap and finished; `Hoard` ran out with the same cap. What is the difference that matters?
hint: How many of each program's arrays are reachable at once?

choices.text: `Hoard`'s arrays are bigger, a megabyte each against a kilobyte
choices.why: Size per object does not matter; `Churn` allocated far more in total.

choices.text: `Churn` keeps one array reachable; `Hoard` keeps every one
choices.why: Right: the list in `pages` held them all, so nothing could be freed.

choices.text: `Hoard` uses an `ArrayList`, which the collector cannot clean
choices.why: The collector cleans lists like anything else once they are unreachable.

choices.text: `Churn` calls the collector itself through a static field
choices.why: A static field is a root; it does not call anything.

prompt: With `-XX:+DisableExplicitGC`, `Request` called `System.gc()` and no collection happened. What does that show?
hint: Compare it with the run without the flag.

choices.text: That the flag broke the program
choices.why: The program printed `asked` and ended normally both times.

choices.text: That the call is a request, and the answer was no
choices.why: Right: same call, no pause; a program must not depend on it.

choices.text: That there was nothing to collect, since `junk` was still reachable
choices.why: `junk = null` made the arrays unreachable before the call.

prompt: The error `Hoard` died with was `java.lang.___: Java heap space`.
`Tidy` overrides `finalize()` and the program printed only `main ends`. Why did `finalize` not run?

choices.text: Because the object was still reachable from `main`
choices.why: `new Tidy()` was never stored; it was garbage at once.

choices.text: Because the compiler removed the method after its warning
choices.why: A warning removes nothing; the method is in the class file.

choices.text: The program ended before any collection, and none happens at exit
choices.why: Right: nobody knows when, or whether, a finaliser runs.

prompt: What does the `[removal]` in `warning: [removal] finalize() in Object has been deprecated and marked for removal` add to an ordinary deprecation?
hint: What will a future JDK do?

choices.text: That the method has already stopped working in Java 25
choices.why: It still compiles and could still be called; removal is announced, not done.

choices.text: That a future release will take it away, not merely discourage it
choices.why: Right: `finalize` has been marked so since Java 18.

choices.text: That the warning only appears with `-Xlint:removal`
choices.why: It appeared with plain `javac`, unasked.

choices.text: That the method was removed from `Object` and `Tidy` defines a new one
choices.why: `Object` still declares it, which is why `@Override` compiled.

prompt: A class holds an open file. What is the main way the course gives for closing it?
hint: At a known point, by the code that opened it.

choices.text: Override `finalize()` to close it
choices.why: Deprecated for removal, and it may never run, as `Tidy` showed.

choices.text: Register it with a `Cleaner`, which closes it promptly
choices.why: A `Cleaner` has the same uncertainty about when; it is only a safety net.

choices.text: A `close()` method the user calls, with try-with-resources
choices.why: Right: lesson 37 makes that hard to forget.

choices.text: Call `System.gc()` after the last use, so the file is collected
choices.why: The collector reclaims memory, not files, and the call is only a request.

prompt: Why is a `Cleaner` acceptable as a backstop when `finalize` was not, if neither says when it runs?
hint: What can each one do to the dying object?

choices.text: Its action cannot resurrect the object, and it is never the main way of closing
choices.why: Right: it backs up a `close()` someone forgot, without the finaliser's ability to revive what it cleans.

choices.text: Because the JVM runs every `Cleaner` action when the program exits
choices.why: No such promise exists; that was exactly `finalize`'s problem too.

choices.text: Because a `Cleaner` runs as soon as the object becomes unreachable
choices.why: It runs some time after, when the collector notices; the timing is just as uncertain.

prompt: A server's memory grows for days until `OutOfMemoryError`. Following the lesson, what do you look for first?
hint: Reachable objects are kept, used or not.

choices.text: A larger `-Xmx`, since the heap is too small
choices.why: More heap delays the error; something that only grows reaches any size.

choices.text: What still holds references it should have dropped
choices.why: Right: usually a collection, often a static one, that only grows.

choices.text: A missing `System.gc()` call in the main loop
choices.why: The collector runs on its own; the call is a request and frees nothing reachable.

choices.text: A class whose `finalize()` is failing
choices.why: Finalisers are deprecated and do not decide what is reachable.

prompt: Match each JVM option used in the lesson to what it did.

pairs.right: Printed a line for every collection

prompt: A cache keeps every `Report` ever produced in a `static Map`, and a report is never looked up again after its first hour. In the lesson's terms, what is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing: reports nobody looks up are unused, so the collector frees them
choices.why: The collector frees the unreachable, not the unused, and a static map is a root.

choices.text: The map should be an instance field, which the collector cleans more often
choices.why: An instance field of a reachable object keeps things just as alive.

choices.text: Every report stays reachable from a root forever, so memory only grows
choices.why: Right: `Hoard` in slow motion; the cache needs to drop old entries.

The JVM's default garbage collector on the lesson's machine, named on the first line of `-Xlog:gc`, is ___.
